storylines.title: The Crown
storylines.about: Told by the King in Rome. The Free Assembly rises against Church and Crown: Virginia in 2767, then the cities of the Crown.

still.caption: The King's study in Rome, by candlelight: the war map on the desk, the dome of Saint Peter's in the window.

lines: Sit by me. The map on the table is the world as it was when I was young.
Everything I am going to tell you began on one plantation in Virginia.
Fairleigh ended it in a single morning, and we called it over.
Look at the map again. The fire did not stay in Virginia.
The clockmaker lost his city in a single night. He thought his machine could think.
He sits in the east wing now and writes to me every week. I read every letter.
The naturalist lost his station in a single night, and thinks it was stolen from him.
He is held in the palace now. I keep him for what he knows of those creatures, and I hear him out.
Lyon went home without a volley. The Cardinal will tell you it was luck. Do not believe him.
The printer named Paris. We should have listened sooner.
I sent Varenne to sea on Fairleigh's word and the Cardinal's prayer.
Remember that mercy is a weapon too. It cuts the one who holds it, sometimes.
Varenne died on the Grève by the King's law, and I signed it.
A martyr is harder to fight than a man. I learnt that too late.
Ferrer's report came before the snow. Machines that take out their own stop-works.
Hollweg kept the broken ones to study. I let him. I wanted to know too.
Ferrer's report came before the snow. Machines that take out their own stop-works.
He had them melted. Hollweg has not forgiven him. I think Ferrer was right.
Rome burned for one night and stood in the morning. I walked the bridges at dawn with Tomasz.
Hollweg and Lindqvist were gone before the bells. I should have held them. I let them go.
I was a seminarian then, waiting for my ship to Rome. I read Augustine under an oak.
The men in the fields talked of an Assembly. I did not understand what they wanted.
I still smell the smoke when I close my eyes.
Two letters came for the Governor that week: one from an explorer in the Amazon, one from a clockmaker. He gave them to me to read.
I spoke on the weavers' square until I had no voice left. Some of them still write to me.
Rouvière would not say who paid him. He said Paris, as if it were a prayer.
I asked for his life and the Marshal gave it. I still do not know if I asked well.
Notre-Dame's doors were black for a year. I made them leave the marks.
I stayed with Varenne the last night. He did not confess. He did let me pray.
Notre-Dame's doors were black for a year. I made them leave the marks.
We counted the people on the steps of Saint Peter's. I knew some of the faces from Mass.
The Romans broke two machines with their bare hands in the Piazza Navona. Nobody had to tell them to.
The harvest is in the barns. A fortune hangs in those rafters, and every rebel in the county knows it.
Study the war table. Then we wait for the night.
It is done. I take no pleasure in it.
Ruggieri has his pipe, and I have the King's leaf. Rome will hear of this.
Paris is quiet. The barricades went back to being carts and paving stones.
Ruggieri wants a dozen more mortars. I have told him he may have six.
The King lets me keep a bench by the window. I do not build. I only take things apart.
Father Ferrer comes on Sundays. He asks me the same question every time.
Ferrer came to Fürth with a notebook and left with a verdict.
I kept the broken ones. I was sure I could mend them. I was sure of a great many things.
Ferrer came to Fürth with a notebook and left with a verdict.
He melted them in my own furnace. I would have learnt what went wrong. Now nobody will.
The council said no machine may govern itself. I said mine did not govern: they served.
Then they woke in the smoke and walked out of the hall without me. I have had a long time to think about that night.
They took my chains off for the King. The guards stay. I do not mind the guards.
Ask me anything about her kind. I am the only man alive who has raised one.
Rome wanted them burned. I walked out of the council and went to the stables, to let them out myself.
Somebody had opened the pens before me. I have never found out who.

storylines.title: The Naturalist
storylines.about: A naturalist on the Amazon raises a creature no one has seen, and loses it to the forest.

still.caption: Dr. Lindqvist's research station on the Rio Negro: the specimen chart on the table, the jars glowing green, rain on the forest outside.

lines: She eats from my hand and follows my whistle. Eleven pounds heavier than Monday.
The Academy wants specimens. I want a breed. The Crown will want a cavalry.
A warehouse at the Barra, crates and charts, and the people who came down the river with me.
He stole her. I will have her line again, whatever the Academy says.
Valadares' report came down the river with him. He saw her, grown, among her own. He writes it as if it were a sorrow.
A nest on the cloud mountain. A Mother, and her young. I must have that mountain.
He would not give the Academy his map. Sealed, for the Holy See. Very well: I have Benedito, and Benedito remembers.
Valadares never came down from the cloud mountain. Benedito came back alone with the canoe, and would not speak of it.
The cages are in the cellar now, and the Academy's men come to look at them through the bars.
They grow. They know my whistle already. This is how it begins, properly this time.
Only a few came down. Few is enough, if they breed.
The carts came down empty. The Academy wants its money back. I will go up again.
Destroyed, the cardinals said. Every one.
I left Rome that night with what I could carry. They will not find the rest.
The commission has gone down the river. I wrote the Storm Sire's hatching hour in the book myself.
Rome calls it a monster. I call it a breed, the first of its line. Every breed needs patience and a good fence.
Valadares said it was made, not born. A Crown man's superstition. Everything that lives was born.
They burned the pens they found. I count the ones that are left every morning. The stud book is thinner.
Valadares said it was made, not born. A Crown man's superstition. Everything that lives was born.
Valadares found half of them and burned them. He wrote that he could smell the rest.
An egg from the plateau under a bell jar, warm to the touch.
Lindqvist writes down its weight every morning. It grows.
A young creature in spirits, coiled like a question. The label says only: Plateau, specimen four.
A crate of straw in the specimen house, scratched from the inside.
Pieter has nailed a second plank over the lid.
A crate under a tarpaulin in the cellar. Lindqvist weighs it every morning.
It grows.
His notes, burned at the edges, on an empty bench.
He copies them out again every night, from memory.

b01_specimen.title: The Warehouse at the Barra
b01_specimen.about: The station is lost. Lindqvist and the survivors are camped in the Academy's warehouse at the Barra do Rio Negro.

still.caption: The Academy's warehouse at the Barra do Rio Negro: crates, jars and charts by lamplight, rain on the river.

a03_plateau.title: The Warehouse at the Barra
a03_plateau.about: Lindqvist reads the mapmaker's report in the Academy's warehouse at the Barra do Rio Negro.

still.caption: The Academy's warehouse at the Barra do Rio Negro: a mapmaker's report open on the table, rain on the river.

a05_specimens.title: The Warehouse at the Barra
a05_specimens.about: The cages from the cloud mountain stand in the Academy's warehouse at the Barra do Rio Negro.

still.caption: The Academy's warehouse at the Barra do Rio Negro: iron cages under lamps, something moving in the straw.

d03_fazenda.title: The Fazenda's Study
d03_fazenda.about: Lindqvist's study in the big house on the island: jars, the stud book, a window on the forest where the pens are.

still.caption: The fazenda's study on the island below Óbidos: the stud book open on the desk, the forest dark in the window.

storylines.title: The Clockmaker
storylines.about: Nuremberg, 2767. A clockmaker builds a machine that never stops, and loses his city to it.

still.caption: Meister Hollweg's workshop in Nuremberg by lantern light: the brass map of the world on its table, the great clock of the Guild.

lines: Mind your sleeve near the table. The map turns, and every ring of it is a road, a river or a sea.
The Crown pays the Guild for patience. My machines have more of it than any soldier.
A barn, a forge and the Crown's goodwill. It is more than we had in December.
The new tower will have a stop-work. Every wheel of it. I will fit it with my own hands.
The line held. The machine went back behind its walls.
The commissary writes his reports. Let him. Our machines are honest.
The Father has gone to Rome with his report. Let him.
The broken ones are under sheets in the back. I will find the fault. Every machine can be mended.
The Father has gone to Rome with his report, and my automata are slag.
He was afraid of them. Fear is not an argument.
No machine may govern itself. Very well: mine will not be governed by Rome either.
Jakob, pack the drawings. We are going south, after the crates.
We are on the river. The bargemen sing at night, and the families sleep among the crates.
At Hamburg we take ship. Nobody there will ask what a clock is for.
The commissary has me. He reads Rome's verdict to me every morning, as if I had not heard it.
(The King: That is not how it went. Hollweg went down the Main, and I let him.)
The great clock of the Guild of the Escapement. It has not lost a second in forty years.
Hollweg says a city could be kept the same way.
The guild's travelling clock, carried out of Nuremberg on the last cart. It keeps the old city's time, and nobody resets it.
The great clock of the Guild still keeps time. It strikes thirteen now.
The travelling clock still keeps Nuremberg's time. Jakob stops it at night now, with his own hand.
The travelling clock rides in a barge's hold, wrapped in sacking. It still keeps Nuremberg's time.
A labouring automaton, half finished. Its hands are a smith's; its face is left blank.
A new labouring automaton on the trestle. A small brass plate on its back reads STOP-WORK FITTED.
The half-finished automaton is gone. Something finished it.
A broken automaton under a sheet. Its stop-work has been fitted again, with a new pin through it.
The trestle is empty. On it lies a receipt from the foundry, signed by Father Ferrer.
The trestle stayed in Fürth. The commissary's men will have found it by now.
Left on the bench, under a gear: I am in Rome. Do not wind anything you find here.
If you are reading this in Nuremberg, you should not be in Nuremberg.

c01_thirteenth.title: The Guild in Exile at Fürth
c01_thirteenth.about: Nuremberg is the machine's. The guild works in a barn at Fürth, three miles west, beside the Crown's army.

still.caption: The guild's barn workshop at Fürth: the brass map saved from Nuremberg on a trestle, the red towers of the lost city through the door.

a02_furth.title: Nuremberg, the Machine's City
a02_furth.about: Hollweg's workshop is the machine's now. He lives in exile in the King's palace in Rome.

still.caption: Hollweg's workshop after the fall: the brass map still turns, and nobody winds it.
